summary: Documents the charter of the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), the body that manages the day-to-day technical work of the IETF. It records how the IESG was understood to operate when it was written. It was later updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717.

plainLanguage.summary: A large working group needs a small leadership team to keep it moving. This memo describes the team that runs the IETF's day-to-day technical work: who is on it, how it makes decisions, how it starts and stops working groups, and how it checks documents before they become RFCs. The author wrote it in 2003 to record how the team already worked, not to set new rules.

subtitle: A written description of what the IESG does to run the IETF and keep its output good.

tldr.problem: The Internet Engineering Steering Group had run the day-to-day technical work of the IETF for years, but no single document described its tasks as they were then understood.
tldr.mechanism: The memo records existing practice: who sits on the IESG, how it reaches decisions, and its roles in working groups, area management, document review and appeals.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational record of practice in spring 2003, not an IETF consensus statement on what the IESG should do, and it has since been updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717.

today: RFC 3710 is an Informational RFC published in February 2004. It has been updated by RFC 3932, RFC 5742 and RFC 8717, and it states that it records IESG practice as understood in 2003 rather than IETF consensus.

sections.title: The Role of the IESG
sections.content:
The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) is the group responsible for the direct operation of the IETF and for ensuring the quality of the work the IETF produces.

Its tasks are laid out in the memo. The IESG charters and terminates working groups, selects their chairs, monitors their progress and coordinates work between them. It performs technical review and approval of working group documents and candidates for the IETF standards track, and it reviews other candidates for publication in the RFC series. It also administers IETF logistics, including operation of the Internet-Draft series and the IETF meeting.

The RFC is candid about its own status. The IESG's role has been largely constant since 1993. At the time of writing, spring 2003, the IETF structure was being reevaluated, so the memo documents existing practice rather than claiming IETF consensus on what the IESG should do. It describes tasks, not the detailed procedures, which live elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG is the leadership team for the IETF. It starts and stops working groups, checks that their documents are good enough to publish, and runs the meetings and the draft series. This memo just writes down the job as it already worked in 2003; it is not a new set of orders.

sections.title: Who Sits on the IESG
sections.content:
The members of the IESG are the IETF Chair, who also acts as the General Area Director when that area is active, and the Area Directors (ADs) for the IETF areas. The IAB Chair and the IETF Executive Director are ex-officio members. The IETF Chair and the ADs are selected by the IETF NomCom under the procedures of BCP 10. The IETF Executive Director is the person charged with running the IETF Secretariat.

The IESG also has liaisons, who are on its mailing list and may attend all its meetings. They exist to speed communication with other bodies in the IETF process, and the IESG decides which positions to have. When the memo was written the liaisons represented the RFC Editor, the IANA and the IAB. Members of the IETF Secretariat are subscribed to the list and attend as needed for support.

Only the IETF Chair and the Area Directors make IESG decisions, though all members can take part in the discussions.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people are full members who decide things, and some are observers and helpers. The full members are the chair and the area directors. The chair of the IAB and the IETF's executive director sit in as non-voting members, and liaisons from other bodies may attend and talk.

sections.title: Decisions, Openness and Confidentiality
sections.content:
The IESG tries to reach every decision unanimously. If it cannot, the chair may conduct informal polls to find consensus. There is no general voting rule; if one were ever needed, the memo expects the IAB rule would apply, where a decision may be taken if at least two thirds of the members concur and there are no more than two dissents. For judging consensus, only the IETF Chair and the Area Directors are counted.

Other procedures may fit particular cases: asserting IETF consensus (for instance on a standards action, with due notice and a chance for community feedback), IESG actions within its own authority, actions by an AD with the advice and consent of the IESG, and independent action by an AD. Decisions can be reached by meeting, teleconference, Internet communication or any combination.

The IESG publishes a record of its decisions and holds an open meeting at every IETF meeting. It also holds private discussions, whose records need not be public; the RFC says this is vital for frank exchange, allowing people to speak freely on controversial topics and to change their minds. Decisions and their reasons are still a matter of public record. Personnel matters, and sometimes legal and financial matters, may be kept confidential, and the chair may exclude members with a conflict of interest or who recuse themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The team aims for agreement. It talks some things over in private so people can speak honestly, but what it decides, and why, is written down for everyone. It meets openly at each IETF meeting. If a vote were ever needed, the rule would be a two-thirds majority with no more than two objections.

sections.title: Working Groups, Areas and Appeals
sections.content:
The IESG manages the working group (WG) process, delegating most of it to the responsible Area Director for each group. A WG chair manages the group from the inside, dealing with people, drafts, meetings and mailing lists. An AD manages it from the outside, dealing with charters, chairs and relationships between groups and areas.

A WG can be requested by community members or initiated by an AD. The AD ensures the proposed group meets the formation criteria in BCP 25, and the charter is negotiated between the AD and the interested community. The AD picks the chairs with the advice of the IESG, but the final decision to charter a WG belongs to the IESG. Terminating a WG is a decision of the responsible AD and is announced with a reason.

The IESG defines the area structure and can add, redefine, merge or close areas, and change how many ADs an area has, in consultation with the community. It can only add new members through the NomCom process. Each area has one or two ADs, who may be advised by directorates. Most decisions of a WG chair can be appealed to the AD, decisions of an individual AD to the IESG, and decisions of the IESG to the IAB; the IAB chair and the IAB liaison recuse themselves from discussion of appeals to the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: Each working group has a chair who runs its daily business. An area director watches several groups from outside, setting their charters and choosing their chairs. If you disagree with a decision, you can appeal it one step up the chain: to the area director, then the IESG, then the IAB.

sections.title: Reviewing Documents
sections.content:
The IESG ensures documents are good enough to be released as RFCs, describe their subject well, and have no outstanding engineering issues. How deep the review goes depends on the intended status and perceived importance of the document.

For standards-track documents that do not come from a working group, the IESG decides whether the specification fits the standards track, whether it needs review by one or more existing working groups, and whether its quality is adequate. No document can be published on the standards track without IESG approval. The IESG may decide that a document should instead be published as Experimental, Informational or a BCP.

Informational and Experimental documents are normally submitted to the RFC Editor, and the IESG reviews them for conflicts with the IETF standards process. It may recommend publishing as-is, review by a working group, publishing with an IESG note, or not publishing. For every document the IESG assigns a specific AD to shepherd it.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a document becomes an official RFC, the team reads it. It can say yes, ask a working group to look again, attach a warning note, or recommend against publishing. For standards, the team also judges whether the topic belongs on the standards track and whether the writing is good enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section says that the security of the Internet depends on standards giving proper thought to security. Apart from that, it states that there seem to be no security considerations relevant to the memo itself.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about how a leadership group is organized, so it has almost nothing to say about computer security. Its one point is that the security of the Internet depends on standards that take security seriously.
